abstract: Alex Imas argues that as AI automates commodity production, economic scarcity shifts from physical goods to relational goods — products and services where human involvement is intrinsic to value. He draws an analogy to agriculture's decline from 40% to 2% of the U.S. workforce, suggesting a comparable structural shift is underway in knowledge work. A central empirical finding comes from an experiment on willingness-to-pay for artwork: human-made art gained 44% in value from exclusivity (one copy vs. many), while AI-generated art gained only 21% — demonstrating that consumers perceive AI creations as inherently reproducible, undermining scarcity premiums. Imas cites Starbucks as a corporate case study: after attempting extensive automation and staff reduction, CEO Brian Niccol reversed course when the strategy hurt customer satisfaction, recognizing that human hospitality — handwritten notes on cups, ceramic cups, great seating — was the actual competitive advantage. The 'relational sector' Imas identifies encompasses care work, education, hospitality, artisanal crafts, entertainment, and spiritual guidance. He grounds the argument in income-elasticity data showing wealthy households spend disproportionately more on these categories, and in economic historians (Comin, Lashkari, Mestieri) showing income effects account for over 75% of sectoral shifts. Baumol's cost disease reinforces the pattern: relational sectors remain expensive precisely because they resist automation.
keyFindings: Human-made art gains 44% in value from exclusivity, versus only 21% for AI-generated art — consumers perceive AI creations as inherently reproducible.
Starbucks reversed its automation strategy after it hurt customer satisfaction, recognizing human hospitality as the competitive advantage.
As AI commoditizes knowledge production, economic value shifts toward the 'relational sector': care, education, hospitality, craft, entertainment.
Income effects account for over 75% of sectoral employment shifts — as real incomes rise from automation, spending reallocates toward high-income-elasticity relational services.
Baumol's cost disease ensures relational sectors remain expensive precisely because they resist automation, naturally absorbing growing expenditure shares.
methodology: Economic essay drawing on experimental evidence (willingness-to-pay studies for human vs. AI art), corporate case studies (Starbucks), income-elasticity data, economic history (Comin, Lashkari, Mestieri on sectoral shifts), and philosophical traditions on mimetic desire (Augustine, Hobbes, Rousseau). Published on Substack.
qualifiers: The art exclusivity experiment is a specific laboratory finding that may not generalize to all relational goods. The Starbucks case is a single corporate example from a specific sector. The relational sector thesis assumes AI will not eventually perform interpersonal and creative work convincingly enough to undermine provenance premiums. A noted counterargument (Philip Trammell) observes that despite centuries of wealth growth, spending on live performers remains near 0%, suggesting new non-relational goods may continuously absorb spending growth. The essay is speculative and forward-looking rather than empirically calibrated.
